01.r: Set the fiftieth year apart as holy, different from ordinary years.
01.n: The intensive form of a verb whose plain form Gesenius gives as TO BE PURE, CLEAN, and then to be holy, sacred; this form means to make holy. It is a perfect with 'and', carrying on the instruction: 'and you shall consecrate'. The 'you' is plural, addressed to the whole people.

02.r: Marks 'the fiftieth year' as the object of 'consecrate'.
02.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted with 'year'.

03.n: Hebrew says 'year' twice: literally 'the year of the fifty, year'. The brief's lexicon lists 'fiftieth' among the uses of the number, and English says 'the fiftieth year' once; both Hebrew words are counted in 'year'. Geneva and YLT keep the doubling: 'that yeere, euen the fiftieth yeere'.

04.r: The fiftieth year, set apart from all others.
04.n: The word is the number 'fifty', with the article, used here as 'fiftieth'.

05.n: The second 'year' of the Hebrew; see the note on the first.

06.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as TO CRY OUT, TO CALL. Another perfect with 'and'.

07.r: Freedom for those bound by debt or sold into service.
07.n: BDB: a flowing, free run, liberty, and it notes the phrase 'proclaim liberty' with this verb; the same word is used of fine, free-flowing myrrh. The Douay-Rheims follows the Latin Vulgate, 'remission'. Who is set free is our reading of the chapter; the verse itself says only 'liberty'.

08.r: Across the whole land of Israel.

10.r: Everyone who lives in the land.
10.n: A participle of the verb 'to sit, dwell': literally 'all its dwellers'.

11.r: The fiftieth year, named after the horn blown to announce it.
11.n: BDB: ram, ram's horn, cornet, and so the name of the fiftieth year, marked by the blowing of cornets. Gesenius thinks it a word imitating a sound, a joyful sound, then a trumpet signal.

12.n: The pronoun is written out, which gives it some emphasis: 'a jubilee it shall be'.

13.r: States what the year is to be.

15.r: Everyone goes back to what is his.
15.n: The ordinary verb 'to turn back, return', plural.

16.n: The word for 'man' used in the sense 'each'.

18.r: The land that belonged to his family.
18.n: Gesenius: possession, especially of lands and fields. This is a different word from 'inheritance' (נַחֲלָה), and our English keeps it apart as 'possession'.

21.r: The extended family he belongs to.
21.n: BDB: clan. Gesenius gives kind, then tribe, and then a subdivision within the people of Israel. It is wider than a household, so 'clan'.

22.r: Repeats the return, now to the family.
22.n: The verb is repeated at the end of the verse, framing the two returns.

01.n: ἁγιάζω, to make holy, as a command: 'and hallow'.

04.n: πεντηκοστός, fiftieth; Pentecost is named from the same word.

05.n: ἐνιαυτός, a year: the Greek, like the Hebrew, says 'year' twice, using two different Greek words.

07.n: ἄφεσις, a release, a letting go; the same word is used in Luke 4:18 on this page, and the New Testament also uses it for forgiveness.

08.n: The second word, τῆς ('the'), has no dictionary form in our data; it is the article ὁ.

10.n: κατοικέω, to dwell in: 'all who dwell in it'.

11.n: The Greek does not keep the Hebrew word: it says 'a year of release, a signal', ἐνιαυτὸς ἀφέσεως σημασία. σημασία, a signal, answers the horn blast behind the Hebrew name.

12.n: Dictionary form supplied; the brief gives none. αὕτη, 'this'.

15.n: Dictionary form supplied; the brief gives none. ἀπελεύσεται, 'he shall go away', singular, with 'each one' as subject.

21.n: πατρίς, fatherland, ancestral home: the Greek reads 'to his ancestral home' for 'his clan'.

22.n: Dictionary form supplied; the brief gives none. ἀπελεύσεσθε, 'you shall go away', plural.
